newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: SOCCER-PORTUGUESE ACT TO CURB SCANDALS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-PORTUGUESE ACT TO CURB SCANDALS.

text.p: Portugal's soccer authorities, battling a series of bribery allegations, have pledged to tighten up rules to prevent a recurrence of the scandals rocking the domestic game.
Promising tough action against anybody found guilty of bribery, the Portuguese Football Federation said on Thursday night that it would introduce new regulations covering the behaviour of referees.
In a statement, the Federation said that it would study "changes to statutes and rules...that can contribute to the prevention of the type of situation that has been seen recently".
The rules would spell out, for example, precisely what referees would be allowed to accept in the way of presents or souvenirs from soccer clubs, it said.

Portuguese soccer has been plunged into crisis by the allegations of attempted match-fixing, with the most serious case involving accusations that Porto sought to bribe a referee ahead of a European match against Aberdeen 12 years ago.
Businessman Fernando Barata has told police that he was asked to approach the Romanian referee in charge of the game and offer him money to secure a 3-0 win for the Portuguese side in the home leg.
Porto won both legs of the 1984 Cup Winners' Cup semifinal 1-0. Both Porto and the match official have denied any bribery attempt was made.
Porto, the reigning Portuguese league champions, are also at the centre of another controversy over the payment of a holiday in Brazil for a leading referee.
The club has officially admitted that it picked up the 700,000-escudo ($4,600) bill but says that it did so without realising who it was for.
UEFA has demanded a thorough investigation of the various charges and accusations.
According to the Lusa news agency, Federation chairman Gilberto Madail will meet UEFA officials in Amsterdam on Monday to brief them on developments.
The crisis has also reinforced calls for sweeping changes to the running of Portuguese soccer, and, in particular, for more independent officials to be appointed to governing bodies.
Portugal's first and second divisions are run by the Portuguese Football League whose top officials can be drawn directly from the clubs.
Pinto da Costa, for example, combines the chairmanship of Porto with that of the League, which has responsibility for the appointment of referees.
The League has already scheduled a special meeting for November 22 when members could vote to bar top officials from being simultaneously directors of individual clubs.
